Proposes an approach (SysSpec: formal-methods-inspired specification + DAG-structured spec patches + LLM agent toolchain; case SpecFS); secondary: compares (generation accuracy vs few-shot 'normal' and 'oracle' baselines across four LLMs, plus ablations, Rust retargeting, productivity, cost and performance evaluations). Also includes a mining study of 3,157 Ext4 commits as motivation

A: SysSpec framework and toolchain (authors' own; agents SpecAssistant, SpecCompiler, SpecReviewer, SpecValidator), version Not stated. Baselines: few-shot 'normal' prompting (file correspondence logic + dependency APIs) and few-shot 'oracle' prompting (+ ground-truth code of dependency modules)

Multi-part specification per module: (1) functionality specification: Hoare-style pre/post-conditions, invariants, system algorithm or intent (levels 1-3 by complexity), in structured natural language with type annotations; (2) modularity specification: Rely-Guarantee interface contracts, modules ≤500 LoC; (3) concurrency specification: locking protocols as pre/post-conditions. Evolution: DAG-structured spec patch (leaf, intermediate, root nodes). Toolchain: shared SysSpec template, role-specific skills, interface pool of Guarantees

Design phase: developer writes specs with SpecAssistant (automated Rely derivation, spec extraction from existing code, NL-guided authoring, spec validation). Implementation phase: SpecCompiler generates each module (sequential version first, then a second pass adds concurrency from the concurrency spec) -> SpecReviewer checks conformance and feeds back until compliant or attempt limit -> SpecValidator system-level cross-module checks and CI-style unit/integration/regression tests; implementation defects go back to the module loop, spec gaps to the developer. Evolution: spec patch applied leaf -> intermediate -> root, implementation regenerated

Developer authors and approves specifications; approves SpecAssistant's suggested refinements; spec gaps found by SpecValidator are reported to the developer and the revised spec must be approved before regeneration; debugging mostly at specification level. C implementation of SpecFS generated 'without any manual intervention'
Full workflow (spec authoring, generation with toolchain, validation, evolution via spec patches); ablations of specification parts and of the Compile-Review loop

Not stated in Böckeler's terms; code is (re)generated from the specification and features are added by patching the spec, not the C code ('shifts the developer's focus from writing low-level code to designing high-level specification'): spec-as-source (classification by the drafter)
New project (SpecFS generated from scratch as a reimplementation of AtomFS's design) and evolution of the generated system (10 Ext4 features via spec patches)

SpecFS: 45 modules, ~4,300 lines of C (ranks 42nd of 82 Linux 6.1.10 file systems by LoC); modules ≤500 LoC (~30K tokens per generation); 10 features = 64 functional modules; xfstests 754 test cases; specifications fewer lines than generated C (Fig. 12)
Systems software: concurrent in-memory FUSE file system (based on the verified AtomFS); Ext4 features
Authors as specification developers; productivity study with two CS master's students and two PhD students; Rust retargeting by a developer without prior Rust experience

Development time in hours (manual vs SysSpec, Table 5); API calls, tokens (cache hit/miss/output) and US$ for one SpecFS generation (Table 6); generation latency (minutes to tens of minutes, qualitative); specification LoC vs C LoC (Fig. 12)

SysSpec 100% vs oracle 81.8% with Gemini-2.5-Pro on AtomFS; SysSpec higher across all models for features (Fig. 11). Ablation: modularity spec lifts concurrency-agnostic modules from 40% to 100%; concurrency spec lifts thread-safe from 0% to 100%. Three Compile-Review passes reach 100% for three models. Productivity 3.0x (Extent) and 5.4x (Rename). Generation under US$1. No significance tests

Distinguished SysSpec from baselines and ablation variants clearly; repeatability not addressed (no repetitions or variance); many values only in Fig. 11; correctness partly by manual inspection. Limitations stated concern SpecFS scope (FUSE, no kernel mode, storage stack or crash consistency; no apples-to-apples performance comparison), not the comparison method

SpecFS is a user-space FUSE file system: no kernel mode, storage stack/direct disk access or crash consistency; no throughput comparison with native file systems. Rust output not idiomatic (C-compatible unsafe style). Simplified specs can sometimes still work (trade-off accuracy vs effort). Upfront design effort higher. Future work: apply to industrial file systems (SpecFS-Ext4 from documentation, starting from Ext2), bootstrap specs from docs/source with SpecAssistant, push-button formal verification integration
